title: Cultural Misunderstandings
summary: We listened to Nok telling her neighbour Tom about a dinner party where things went wrong because of cultural differences. We learned expressions like put your foot in it and split the bill. We used would have, should have and could have to give advice about things in the past.

grammar.title: Past modals: would have, should have, could have
grammar.explain: We use these modals + have + past participle to talk about the past. They give advice or comments about something that already happened and can't be changed. Should have = it was the right thing, but you didn't do it; could have = another possible choice; would have = what I would do in your place.
grammar.explain_ar: نستخدم هذه الأفعال المساعدة + have + التصريف الثالث للفعل للحديث عن الماضي، لتقديم نصيحة أو تعليق على شيء حدث ولا يمكن تغييره. should have = كان هذا هو الصواب لكنك لم تفعله، could have = كان هناك خيار آخر ممكن، would have = ما كنتُ سأفعله لو كنت مكانك.
form: should / shouldn't + have + past participle: You shouldn't have asked her about her age.
could + have + past participle: You could have explained that sharing is common in your country.
would + have + past participle: I would have called him.
It would have been better + to + verb: It would have been better to pay her a compliment.
Question: Couldn't you have + past participle? – Couldn't you have used your credit card?

examples.en: I probably would've called him to tell him I was running late.
examples.note: Tom says what he would do in Nok's place.

examples.en: You probably shouldn't have asked her about her age.
examples.note: Nok asked, and it was a mistake.

examples.en: It would've been better to pay her a compliment.
examples.note: A better choice in the past.

examples.en: Maybe you could've explained that sharing dishes is common where you come from.
examples.note: Another possible action she didn't take.

examples.en: Couldn't you have used your credit card?
examples.note: Question suggesting a possible solution in the past.

mistakes.wrong: You could've take off your shoes.
mistakes.right: You could've taken off your shoes.
mistakes.why: After have, use the past participle (taken), not the base form.
'Should've' sounds like 'should of', but we write have.

mistakes.right: You shouldn't have asked her age.

mistakes.why: The form is would + have + past participle.

quiz.q: She was upset. You ___ asked about her salary.
quiz.why: Shouldn't have = it was a mistake to do it.

quiz.q: You were late. You ___ called to say you were running late.
quiz.why: Should have + past participle = the right thing you didn't do.

quiz.q: If I were you, I ___ checked how the bill was being paid.
quiz.why: Would have = what I would do in your situation in the past.

quiz.q: It would've been better ___ her a compliment.
quiz.why: It would have been better + to + verb.

quiz.q: You didn't have enough cash. ___ used your credit card?
quiz.why: Question form: Couldn't you have + past participle?

grammar.title: Adverbs of certainty with advice
grammar.explain: Words like probably, definitely, possibly and perhaps (or maybe) show how sure we are about our advice. They make the advice softer or stronger, so it sounds more polite.
grammar.explain_ar: كلمات مثل probably و definitely و possibly و perhaps (أو maybe) تُظهر مدى تأكّدنا من نصيحتنا. فهي تجعل النصيحة ألطف أو أقوى، فتبدو أكثر تهذيباً.
form: subject + probably / definitely + would / should + have: I probably would've called.
subject + probably / definitely + shouldn't + have: You probably shouldn't have asked.
Maybe / Perhaps at the start: Maybe you could've explained.
softer: perhaps, maybe, possibly – stronger: definitely

examples.en: You probably shouldn't have asked her about her age.
You definitely should've paid her a compliment.
Perhaps you could've left a little food on your plate.
You could possibly have phoned the host.

mistakes.why: Put probably before a negative modal (shouldn't).

mistakes.right: I would probably have called him.
mistakes.why: Keep have + past participle after the adverb.

quiz.why: Definitely shows you are very sure.

quiz.q: Choose the correct order: You ___ asked her age.
quiz.why: The adverb goes before a negative modal.

quiz.q: ___ you could have explained the custom to her.
quiz.why: Maybe/Perhaps at the start makes a soft suggestion.

quiz.q: Why do we use adverbs like probably with advice?
options: To show how sure we are and sound softer
quiz.why: They change how strong the advice is.

quiz.q: I ___ called him to say I was running late.
quiz.why: In positive sentences, put probably before the modal: I probably would've called.

phrases.en: I really put my foot in it!

phrases.use: Saying what you would have done
Suggesting a better choice in the past
Asking about a possible solution in the past

phrases.en: Sorry, I'm running late. I'll be there in 20 minutes.
phrases.use: Telling a host you will be late

phrases.en: It's on me. / It's my treat.
